summary: A small woodpecker of old, open pine forest, and the only one that carves its home in living pines.
description: A small black-and-white woodpecker about 9 inches long, with a barred back, white underparts spotted black along the flanks, a black crown, and large white cheek patches.  The male has a small red mark near the crown that is seldom seen.
habitat: Mature, open pine forest, mostly longleaf, with trees usually more than 80 years old.
life: It lives in small family groups that raise the young together.  It digs its nest cavity in a living pine, often one softened by red-heart disease, and the work can take years.  It keeps resin flowing around the hole, which wards off rat snakes.
alabama: It lives in Alabama where mature, open pine forest remains.  The state's wildlife agency notes that its numbers fell sharply as the longleaf forests were cut, and that biologists now add artificial nest boxes to help it.  The sources read for this entry do not name the places, so see the status assessment for the populations.
countiesText: Not named in the sources read
range: Scattered populations from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas and Oklahoma
notes: Listed as endangered in 1970, and reclassified as threatened by a rule published October 25, 2024 (89 FR 85337).

seasonNote: In Alabama from about August to May, with the most birds in winter
summary: A small, sand-colored shorebird that winters on the islands at the mouth of Mobile Bay.
description: A small shorebird about 7 inches long, sandy brown above and white below, with orange legs.  In breeding dress it has a black band across the forehead, another across the breast, and an orange bill tipped black.  In winter, when Alabama sees it, the bands are gone and the bill is black.
habitat: Sandy beaches and tidal flats on the coast.  Inland, it nests on the bare shores of lakes and on river sandbars.
life: It picks small invertebrates from the surface of the sand.  The chicks feed themselves from the day they hatch.
alabama: A winter visitor.  The chief sites are Pelican Island, Little Dauphin Island, and parts of Dauphin Island, with occasional birds at the western tip of the Fort Morgan Peninsula.  Fewer than 40 usually winter in the state at once, where more than 200 once did.
range: Breeds on the Atlantic coast, the Great Lakes, and the northern Great Plains; winters on the southern Atlantic and Gulf coasts
threats: In Alabama: loss of habitat, disturbance by people, predators, and the decline of the tidal flats where it feeds.
notes: The birds of the Great Lakes are listed separately, as endangered.  Those from the Atlantic coast and the northern Great Plains are threatened.

summary: A stocky sandpiper that flies as far as 19,000 miles a year between the Arctic and the far south.
description: A stocky shorebird 9 to 11 inches long with a short black bill.  In spring its face and underparts are rusty red.  In winter it is pale gray above and white below.
habitat: Coastal bays, estuaries, and tidal flats.  It nests on dry Arctic tundra near fresh water.
life: It is among the longest-distance migrants known.  It eats mostly small hard-shelled mollusks, and in spring the eggs of horseshoe crabs.
alabama: A bird of the coast in migration and in winter.  The Service places part of its wintering range in the southeastern United States, from Alabama to North Carolina.
range: Breeds in the central Canadian Arctic; winters from the southeastern United States and the Gulf to the tip of South America
threats: Too few safe places to rest at high tide, disturbance by people, and falcons.  The recovery plan covers the wider threats.

summary: A sparrow-sized marsh bird, the smallest rail in North America, and one almost never seen.
description: A tiny rail, 4 to 6 inches long, gray-black with white speckles on the back, a chestnut nape, a short tail, red eyes, and a black bill.
habitat: Dense marsh cover over moist soil or very shallow water, in salt, brackish, and fresh marshes.
life: It is secretive.  It runs through the vegetation where another bird would fly, and the males may call by day or by night.
alabama: Alabama lies within its range on the Gulf coast, but the Service found no credible records from the state between 2010 and 2017.  Texas and Florida are its strongholds on the Gulf.
range: The Atlantic and Gulf coasts, parts of the Great Plains, the Caribbean, and south to Brazil
threats: Loss and breaking up of marshes, changes to their water, a rising sea, contaminants, predators, and disturbance by people.

summary: The tallest bird in North America, a few of which now winter each year at Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge.
description: A white crane about 5 feet tall, with a wingspan of more than 7 feet, black wingtips, a red crown, and a dark gray patch on the nape.
habitat: Marshes, shallow lakes and bays, wet meadows, rivers, and farm fields.
life: Whooping cranes pair for life and can live more than 30 years in the wild.  A pair usually lays two eggs.
alabama: Whooping cranes have wintered at Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge every year since 2006, when two birds from a reintroduced flock turned up there.  As many as 29 were counted in the winter of 2017 to 2018.  They are often seen near the refuge's visitor center.
countiesText: Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge, in the Tennessee Valley
range: One self-sustaining wild flock, which migrates between Texas and Canada, and reintroduced flocks in the East
threats: Loss of wetlands, development, power lines, wind farms, and drought.
notes: The species as a whole has been listed as endangered since March 11, 1967 (32 FR 4001).  The cranes that reach Alabama belong to the eastern migratory flock, which was set up in 2001 as a nonessential experimental population under a special rule.

summary: The great woodpecker of the old southern forests, lost from Alabama and not surely seen anywhere since 1944.
description: A very large black-and-white woodpecker, about 19 to 20 inches long with a wingspan of 30 inches or more.  It had a white, chisel-tipped bill, a lemon-yellow eye, and a pointed crest, red in the male and black in the female.
habitat: Very large forests with many big, dying trees.
alabama: Alabama's wildlife agency counts the ivory-bill among the woodpeckers lost from the state.  The sources read for this entry do not say where in Alabama it lived or when it was last seen here.
range: Once the forests of the Southeast, from the Carolinas to Texas and north along the Mississippi
threats: The Service gives its last accepted sighting as April 1944, in the Singer Tract of northeast Louisiana.  It needed forest of a size and age that is all but gone.
